source.title: Risk and Rizq
source.summary: How Islamic concepts of divine provision and chance gave the world the vocabulary of uncertainty, insurance, and entrepreneurship.
source.author: Islamic Economics
source.body_text: The word "hazard" comes from al-zahr, Arabic for dice. Explore how the Islamic concept of rizq (divine provision) created a culture of entrepreneurial risk-taking, how the prohibition of gharar (excessive uncertainty) shaped contract ethics, and how Khadijah bint Khuwaylid embodied the merchant spirit. From mudaraba partnerships to modern takaful insurance, now a $50 billion industry.

linkedin.post: The word "hazard" traces back to al-zahr — Arabic for dice. It's a perfect metaphor for how Islamic civilization gave the world its vocabulary of risk and uncertainty. Islamic contracts prohibited gharar (excessive uncertainty) not to avoid risk, but to ensure fairness. You could sell wheat growing in your field, but not wheat you merely hoped to plant next year. The distinction was crucial: legitimate business risk versus exploitative speculation. Khadijah bint Khuwaylid exemplified this merchant spirit, running trade caravans across Arabia through mudaraba partnerships that split profits between capital and labor without guaranteeing returns. This culture of ethical risk-taking evolved into modern takaful insurance, now a $50 billion industry based on risk-sharing rather than risk-transfer. From medieval trading partnerships to contemporary Islamic finance, the principles remain constant: embrace uncertainty, but structure it fairly. Listen: https://islamiceconomics.github.io/podcast.html#ep-tt-5
